questions.q: Does Llama-AVSR beat prior SOTA under matched labeled-hour budgets on LRS3, and is VSR included in that claim?
questions.answer: ASR yes (0.79% @1756h; 1.1% @433h; 1.5% @30h all below prior best at comparable budgets, e.g. auto-avsr 1.0/1.0 @1902/3448h, RAVEn 1.9/1.4 and BRAVEn 1.7/1.1 @30/433h). AVSR yes (0.95% @433h and 0.77% @1756h vs auto-avsr 1.0/0.9 @1902/3448h and Fast Conformer 0.9 @1687h). VSR no: 25.3% @433h trails RAVEn 24.4% and BRAVEn 20.1%; only beats LLM-based VSP-LLM (26.7%) and auto-avsr (36.3%); at 1756h 24.0% is claimed 'parity' with auto-avsr (1902h, 23.5%) and RAVEn (433h, 24.4%), not superiority. The paper concedes this and scopes its SOTA claims to ASR and AVSR.

questions.q: Can the headline WERs be reproduced or trusted statistically?
questions.answer: No: a single WER per cell is reported with no seeds, repetitions, standard deviations, or confidence intervals; the LRS3 evaluation partition, utterance count, and speaker set are never stated; WER text normalization is unstated; checkpoint/hyperparameter selection data are unstated; and no code or configs are public. Any of these could move the headline numbers.

questions.q: Is the paper internally consistent between its text and Table I?
questions.answer: No. Sec. III-B writes 'outperforms the other methods when using 433 and 30 hours achieving WER results of 1.5% and 1.1%, respectively', which pairs 433h with 1.5% and 30h with 1.1%, but Table I lists 30h = 1.5% (K=2) and 433h = 1.1% (K=3). Similarly, the text's caveat 'Llama-AVSR outperforms the other methods' is only loosely matched to Table I for VSR (worse than RAVEn/BRAVEn).

questions.q: Does adding the visual modality actually help, and when?
questions.answer: At 433h, AVSR (0.95%) beats ASR (1.1%); the gain is small and shrinks with more data (1756h: 0.79% ASR -> 0.77% AVSR, which the authors flag as reduced, 'in line with previous works'). Under babble noise the visual stream is decisive: the ASR-only Table III row collapses to 63.1% WER at -5 dB while AVSR rows hold at 16.4-18.2% (e.g. K=4/2: 16.9%; A2V4: 18.2%).

questions.q: Is the claim 'outperforms methods that exploit tens of thousands of hours' supported?
questions.answer: Only partially. vs ViT3D-CM (90K h, 1.6%) both AVSR results win. vs LP Conformer (100K h, 0.9%), Llama-AVSR at 433h (0.95%) is worse; only the 1756h run (0.77%) beats it. The 433h AVSR number (0.95%) also loses to Fast Conformer at 1687h (0.9%) and ties auto-avsr at 3448h (0.9%).

questions.q: Is the comparison against the fine-tuned Whisper baseline apples-to-apples?
questions.answer: No. The Whisper-finetuned baseline (2.3%) is a fully fine-tuned Whisper-Large (1550M params, >1.5B updated) whereas Llama-AVSR uses a frozen Whisper-medium with 42M trainable params; the authors themselves concede the Whisper-size mismatch. The comparison demonstrates parameter efficiency at the same task family, not a matched-capacity win.

questions.q: Could evaluation leak via pre-training or pseudo-labels?
questions.answer: Unverifiable from the paper: AV-HuBERT is pre-trained on 'LRS3 + VoxCeleb2' (sentence split across the page break) with no split detail, and VoxCeleb2 transcripts are Whisper pseudo-labels following [4] with no filtering, confidence threshold, or surviving-hour count given; speaker overlap between training and the (unstated) LRS3 test split is not addressed either.

questions.q: What do the authors concede as weaknesses?
questions.answer: (1) VSR trails RAVEn/BRAVEn - 'the gap ... is more noticeable'; (2) linear projectors are a bottleneck and better ones are left to future work (VSR gap); (3) not compressing video tokens yields no gain except in severe noise; (4) video's marginal gain shrinks with data (0.79%->0.77%); (5) AV-HuBERT for both modalities is slightly worse; (6) VSR degrades ~2.5-3 points if pushed to K=5; (7) Llama2-7B's LoRA gain is reduced vs TinyLlama; (8) conclusion: VSR only at best 'comparable' to prior works.

questions.q: Are Fig. 2 and Table II enough to support the LoRA / encoder / LLM-size claims?
questions.answer: Only weakly. Text anchors just the four TinyLlama values (4.04/3.81% -> 2.31/1.70% with LoRA); the other eight Fig. 2 WERs are figure-only, with the marker-to-value mapping inferred from the listing order and the legend groups (WavLM then Whisper), and should be verified against the PDF. Table II does show LoRA placement helps (28.3/25.3 LLM+enc vs 30.2/28.4 no-LoRA) but on a single run with no variance.

questions.q: What should a skeptical reviewer ask the authors for?
questions.answer: The LRS3 evaluation split and speaker counts, repetitions/seeds with variance, the WER normalization tool, the checkpoint-selection protocol, matched-budget re-evaluation of auto-avsr/RAVEn/LP Conformer under this exact protocol, noise-evaluation seeds for Table III, decoding details (length penalty, prompt identity at eval), and public code/configs/checkpoints.

questions.q: Is there any evidence the evaluation used the same prompt and decoding as training?
questions.answer: Not stated. The training prompt is given ('Transcribe {task_prompt} to text.' with task_prompt in {speech, video, speech and video}) and decoding is beam search width 15 at temperature 0.6, but the paper never says whether evaluation used the identical prompt, nor the length penalty, repetition handling, max tokens, or stop criteria.

questions.q: Does the paper address confirmation, correction, grounding, or deployment costs (M08/M09/M10/M13)?
questions.answer: No. Outputs are raw transcription text with no confidence scores, timestamps, or n-best lists; there is no confirmation (M09) or correction/error-recovery (M10) mechanism, and no deployment numbers (latency, throughput, memory, real-time factor, streaming vs offline) anywhere. Error analysis is WER only.

questions.q: Does the VSR comparison with VSP-LLM in Table I use VSP-LLM's matched configuration?
questions.answer: No. Table I lists VSP-LLM at 26.7% (frozen visual encoder); VSP-LLM's own Table 1 also reports VSP-LLM(FT) at 25.4% with an unfrozen encoder, the configuration that matches Llama-AVSR's video-encoder LoRA (25.3%).
